claims.text: A machine-learning model integrating first-principles phonon-scattering descriptors will predict low phonon thermal conductivity in HEAs more accurately than current DFT-based or empirical models.
The proposed model's accuracy advantage will be especially pronounced in HEAs with high configurational disorder.
The target materials are solid-solution, multi-principal-element HEAs with equimolar or near-equimolar compositions.
Each element in the target HEAs is present at 5–35 at.%.
The target solid-solution HEAs exhibit significant local lattice distortion.
First-principles phonon-scattering descriptors can capture multi-element interactions and local lattice distortions in HEAs.
Combining computed descriptors with machine learning trained on a systematic HEA composition dataset is a suitable strategy for exploring HEA composition space.
The proposed model is to be evaluated using thermal-conductivity measurements over approximately 300–800 K.
High configurational disorder gives rise to local lattice distortions and complex phonon-scattering pathways in HEAs.
Machine learning can exploit nonlinear correlations between phonon-scattering descriptors and measured thermal conductivity.
Traditional DFT-based and empirical models overlook scattering channels associated with severe lattice distortion and chemical disorder in HEAs.
Capturing these additional scattering channels will enhance the model's predictive power.
The proposed model will reduce prediction error by approximately 15–25% relative to current DFT-based or empirical methods.
The approach is expected to apply primarily to equimolar or near-equimolar solid-solution HEAs between 300 and 800 K.
The model may not generalize reliably to extreme compositional deviations or non-equilibrium phases.
Systematic experimental validation across a representative set of HEA compositions is required to determine the precise error reduction.
A systematic experimental series can compare the proposed model's prediction errors with those of conventional DFT-based or empirical methods.
Failure to achieve at least a 15% statistically significant reduction in prediction error would falsify the hypothesis.
